sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Phoíbē** (*phoebe*) — Titaness of Prophecy · Bright, shining — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Titaness of Prophecy". The name means "Bright, shining"[^1].

Phoíbē is the **Titaness of prophecy**, the 'shining one' whose name is simply the feminine of φοῖβος, 'bright'. Before Apollo ever spoke at Delphi, the Pythia's own prayer names her the oracle's **third keeper** — after Gaia and Themis — who passed the seat to her grandson as a birthday gift. She is **light as foresight**: the radiance that sees before it shines.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Phoíbē** and serves its temple at [phoíbē.com](https://xn--phob-xpa3u.com). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *phoebe* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.
Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Greek as **Φοίβη**. Etymologically it means "Bright, shining"[^1].

The ASCII form *phoebe* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Phoíbē** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **p** → **P** — P uppercase
- **h** → **h** — h same
- **o** → **o** — o same
- **e** → **í** — Special character
- **b** → **b** — b same
- **e** → **ē** — Macron: long vowel

The project holds the domain **phoíbē.com** (xn--phob-xpa3u.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/pʰóɪ.bɛː/** — Attic Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Phoi-** — aspirated pʰ — a 'p' released with breath, not an English 'f' — plus the diphthong oi as in οἶκος; the acute accent means the voice rises across this syllable
- **-bē** — voiced b followed by long eta (η), an open 'eh' held twice the length of a short vowel — never the English 'ee' the modern name has drifted to

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'FOY-beh' — the first syllable rhymes with 'boy' and carries the rising pitch; the second is a long, open 'eh', not 'bee'.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — φοῖβος (phoîbos), 'bright, shining, pure' — the masculine form, Apollo's standing epithet, which Aeschylus derives outright from her name (Eumenides 7–8)
- **PIE** — *bʰeh₂- 'to shine, appear' (compare φαίνω, 'to bring to light', φάος, 'light') — proposed but contested; Beekes and Chantraine both treat the derivation cautiously

Tier-1: the Greek Φοίβη carries both an accent (the acute on the diphthong οί) and a long vowel (η), so the restoration Phoíbē preserves stress and quantity together — two facts of the name that plain ASCII 'Phoebe' silently erases.

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Phoíbē concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **Golden Crown** — Hesiod's sole epithet for her in the Titan catalogue — Φοίβην τε χρυσοστέφανον, 'Phoebe of the golden crown' (Theogony 136): the royalty of the eldest generation, and light worn on the brow.
- **Delphic Tripod** — The Pythia's three-legged seat at Delphi, which Aeschylus' succession makes hers third, after Gaia and Themis (Eumenides 1–8) — the one concrete object to which her mythic tenure attaches.
- **Omphalos** — The navel-stone marking Delphi as the center of the world; part of the sanctuary landscape of the oracle she held and handed on. She has no independent iconography — her attributes are Delphi's.
- **Laurel** — The prophetic tree of Delphi, inherited by Apollo together with the seat she gave him; with her it marks the continuity of the shrine rather than a personal emblem.
- **Prophetic Radiance** — Her name itself — the feminine of φοῖβος, 'bright, shining' — is her symbol: light understood as foresight, the gleam that sees ahead.
- **The Moon** — A late association: Roman poets use Phoebē as a name of the moon paired with Phoebus the sun, and through her granddaughter Artemis she drifts lunar. Ancient, but poetic rather than cultic.

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Phoíbē stands quietly at the hinge of Greek myth: a Titan of the eldest generation whose role is to inherit and to hand on — the oracle to Apollo, the bloodline to Leto. Her myths are genealogies that glow: everything she touches passes light forward.[^1]

### Golden-Crowned among the Titans (Hesiod)

In the *Theogony* (132–136), Hesiod catalogues the twelve Titans born to Ouranos and Gaia — Ocean, Koios, Krios, Hyperion, Iapetus, Theia, Rheia, Themis, Mnemosyne, Tethys, and Kronos — and among them 'Phoíbē of the golden crown' (Φοίβην τε χρυσοστέφανον). She is one of the few in the list to carry an epithet at all, and hers is an epithet of light. Hesiod records no deed of hers; the eldest Titans are not actors but origins, the generation from which the Olympian world descends.[^2]

### The Much-Desired Couch of Koios (Hesiod)

Later in the *Theogony* (404–410), Phoíbē 'ascended the much-desired couch of Koios' (Φοίβη δ' αὖ Κοίου πολυήρατον ἷξε λέχος εἰσαναβᾶσα) and conceived Leto — 'dark-robed, gentle, the mildest of all who dwell on Olympus'. The line continues without pause: Leto bears 'Apollo and arrow-pouring Artemis' to Zeus (*Theogony* 918–920), so Phoíbē stands at the head of the Delphic family, grandmother to the two Olympians of light. Hesiod gives the marriage no quarrel and no story beyond the bed and the child; for a Titaness of the first generation, the genealogy is the myth.

### The Third Voice of Delphi (Aeschylus)

The opening lines of Aeschylus' *Eumenides* (1–8) preserve her greatest role. The Pythia, praying at Delphi, names Gaia 'first of prophets' and Themis second upon her mother's seat; third — 'with her consent, and by no violence' — sat 'another Titan, a child of Earth, Phoíbē'. Phoíbē then gave the throne to Apollo 'as a birthday gift' (γενέθλιον δόσιν), 'and he bears his name Phoíbos as a namesake from hers' (τὸ Φοίβης δ' ὄνομ' ἔχει παρώνυμον). It is the only peaceful succession in the violent history of the Greek gods: the oracle changes hands as a family inheritance, and the new god's famous epithet is, the tragedian insists, simply his grandmother's name.

### Two Daughters of Prophecy (Apollodorus)

Apollodorus (*Library* 1.4.1) gives her motherhood its full shape: from Koios and Phoíbē spring two daughters, Asteria and Leto. Asteria, 'the starry one', bears Hekátē to Perses (*Theogony* 409–412), the torch-bearing goddess of crossroads whom Zeus honors above all; Leto bears Apollo and Artemis. Through one daughter flows the lineage of night sky and moonlight, through the other the lineage of sunlit prophecy: both of Delphi's lights, in effect, are Phoíbē's grandchildren.

sources.citation: Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Phoíbē never received a Roman cult of her own; Rome met her inside Apollo, whose Greek epithet Phoebus became a standard poetic name — and whose name Aeschylus had already declared to be hers (Eumenides 7–8). In Latin poetry the feminine Phoebē then hardens into a name of the moon itself, paired with Phoebus the sun, so the Titaness survives in Rome as a word rather than a worship. Through her granddaughter Artemis–Diana, later poets quietly fold her into the lunar goddess, but the equation remains poetic, never cultic, and no ancient author confuses the two genealogies.[^1]

Within the Greek tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[adamas|Adámas]], [[aer|Aḗr]], [[aither|Aithḗr]], and [[ananke|Anánkē]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: The name lives on in English as **Phoebe** — entering the Christian tradition through Phoíbē of Cenchreae, the deaconess Paul commends to the Roman church (Romans 16:1) — and it has been one of the most durable classical given names in the language ever since. Astronomy keeps the Titaness herself: **Phoebe**, the dark retrograde outer moon of Saturn discovered by W. H. Pickering in 1899, is named for her, a fitting moon for the Titaness of light. And whenever literature writes 'Phoebus Apollo', it repeats — whether it knows it or not — her name, which Aeschylus says Apollo took from his grandmother. The small American flycatcher called the phoebe, by contrast, is named for its call: a false friend, not a descendant.[^1]

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Phoíbē has no temple, sanctuary, or cult image of her own anywhere in the Greek world — she belongs to genealogy and to Delphi's remembered past rather than to ritual. Her setting is the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi, where French excavations since 1892 have uncovered the Archaic and Classical temples above the adyton in which the Pythia sat, the very seat whose pre-Apolline tenants the Pythia lists in Aeschylus' prologue; Pausanias (10.5.5–7) records the parallel Delphic tradition of an older oracle of Earth and Themis, passed on until Apollo held it. The omphalos copies and tripod dedications in the Delphi museum are the material shadow of the throne she is said to have kept third.[^1]

sources.citation: Pausanias, Description of Greece, Loeb Classical Library, 180.

sections.label: Homeric Hymns
sections.body: No Homeric Hymn to Phoíbē survives, and none was likely ever sung: the collection passes over her entirely, as it does most of the Titanides — among the elder gods only Hélios and Selḗnē received hymns of their own (Hymns 31 and 32), both short and both late.[^1] Her literary life runs instead through two channels that need no hymn: the genealogy of Hesiod, where she is born a daughter of Ouranós and Gaîa and becomes the wife of Koíos, mother of Lētṓ and Astériā,[^2] and the Delphic pre-history staged by Aeschylus, where the Pythia names her third holder of the oracle, who surrendered the seat to Apollo 'as a birthday gift' (γενέθλιον δῶρον).[^3] The silence of the hymnic corpus is therefore not a loss but a datum: Phoíbē is a functional goddess, preserved in memory chiefly because her name explains her grandson's. A temple is the stronger for saying so plainly.

sources.citation: Homeric Hymns 31 and 32 (to Helios and Selene), the collection's only hymns to elder gods.
Hesiod, Theogony 132–136 and 404–410 (Phoebe among the Titans; her union with Coeus).
Aeschylus, Eumenides 1–8 (the Pythia's prologue: the Delphic succession).

sections.label: Epithets & Epicleses
sections.body:
Phoíbē never drew a cult, so her 'epithets' are not a hymnic inventory but the biography of a single name moving down the generations — from a Titan daughter of Earth, through the Delphic succession, to her grandson, and at last to the moon.

- **Φοίβη** (*Phoibē*) — 'shining, bright,' the feminine of φοῖβος; her own name among the twelve Titans, Hesiod, Theogony 136.[^1]
- **Τιτανίς** (*Titanis*) — 'the Titaness, a child of Earth'; how the Pythia introduces her at Delphi, Aeschylus, Eumenides 6.[^2]
- **Φοῖβος** (*Phoibos*) — the masculine form, inherited by her grandson as his most constant epic epithet (already Iliad 1.44, Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων) and expressly derived from Phoíbē at Eumenides 8, 'who has his name from her' (τοὔπώνυμον).[^3]
- **Φοίβη** of the moon — in later poetry the name drifts to Selḗnē and the moon-goddess; so repeatedly in Nonnus, Dionysiaca.[^4]

sources.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 136 (Phoebe in the catalogue of Titans).
Aeschylus, Eumenides 6–8 (Τιτανίς … παῖς Χθονός; Φοῖβος named from Φοίβη).
Homer, Iliad 1.44 (Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων).
Nonnus, Dionysiaca (Phoibe applied to the moon, passim).

sections.label: Oracle & Cult Sites
sections.body: Delphi is the only oracular seat ever claimed for Phoíbē, and the claim is literary before it is cultic. In the prologue of the Eumenides the Pythia traces the shrine's succession: first Gaîa, then Thémis, then third, 'by consent and under no compulsion,' another Titan, a child of Earth, Phoíbē, who gave the mantic seat to Phoîbos Apollo as a birthday gift.[^1] Euripides knows a harsher version: after Apollo takes the oracle, Gaîa sends dream-prophecies in protest until Zeus silences them at the young god's plea — a version in which Phoíbē plays no part.[^2] Pausanias, reporting the Delphians' own account, likewise omits her, passing the oracle from Earth to Themis and from Themis to Apollo.[^3] Her place in the chain is thus essentially Aeschylean theology, devised to explain the name Phoîbos. No temple, altar, or priesthood of Phoíbē is attested at Delphi or anywhere else; the first generation of gods may be said to hold everything, and to keep nothing.

sources.citation: Aeschylus, Eumenides 1–8 (Gaia → Themis → Phoebe → Phoebus; the 'birthday gift').
Euripides, Iphigenia among the Taurians 1234–1283 (the choral prehistory of Delphi; the dream-oracles).
Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.5.5–6 (the Delphic succession without Phoebe).

sections.label: Iconography
sections.body:
Phoíbē has no iconographic type of her own: Pausanias records no statue, no source assigns her an attribute, and her rare appearances in art depend entirely on labels for their identification.

- **Pergamon Altar, south frieze** (c. 180–160 BC; Pergamonmuseum, Berlin) — a goddess inscribed ΦΟΙΒΗ fights a winged giant beside her daughter Astériā; the incised names, not any attribute, secure the pair.[^1]
- **No fixed attributes** — unlike Lētṓ with her veil and twin children, or her grandson with bow, laurel, and lyre, she bears nothing in particular; she is a name rendered visible, not an image rendered recognizable.
- **Absent from Delian birth scenes** — the Attic and later vases of Lētṓ's labor with the palm and the twin births exclude her; compare the catalogue of birth scenes in LIMC s.v. 'Leto'.[^2]
- **Lunar drift** — once her name passed to the moon, her visual identity was absorbed into Selḗnē's; the crescent, billowing veil, and torch of late antique lunar imagery belong to Selḗnē, not to the Titaness.[^3]

sources.citation: LIMC VII.1 (1994), s.v. 'Phoibe' (Pergamon Altar, south frieze).
Pergamonmuseum, Berlin, the Great Altar (c. 180–160 BC), south frieze: inscribed figures of Asteria and Phoebe.
LIMC VI.1 (1992), s.v. 'Leto' (the iconography of the Delian birth).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Phoíbē is nearly invisible in Greek worship, and that invisibility is the point: her significance is structural rather than devotional. She is the lawful transmission of prophecy. In a myth-world built on violent succession — Ouranos castrated by Kronos, Kronos overthrown by Zeus — Aeschylus makes hers the sole peaceful one: the oracle passes 'with consent and by no violence', as a gift, and even leaves its name behind as a family inheritance. The Greeks seem to have felt that foresight, unlike kingship, could not be seized; it had to be bequeathed. Her shining is therefore not the blaze of the sun but the quiet lamp of knowledge kept burning across generations — from Earth, through law in Themis, through her, into Apollo's daylight.[^1]
